say.text: A 9-year-old boy has had a cold for 3 days, then 10 hours of pain in the right lower abdomen. Your registrar asks what is blocking his appendix.
Which is the **most likely** obstruction?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with his age. Which obstruction is common in a child, and which in an adult?
Tempting: the faecolith is the cause you probably learned first, and it shows well on CT.
But look at the age in the stem. Where is the lymphoid tissue of the appendix largest?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause on this: the age in the stem decides the cause, not the cause you know best.

say.text: Faecoliths predominate in adults (K15). Lymphoid tissue is richest in young people and atrophies with age (K23).
So in a child, lymphoid hyperplasia, often after a viral illness, is the usual blocker (K14).
Yes. In a child the lymphoid tissue swells, often after a viral illness, and blocks the lumen (K14).
Let's walk one case all the way, with the reasoning shown. This is the worked case: the 9-year-old.
Step 1, the lumen. Obstruction is the usual starting event, and here it is lymphoid hyperplasia (K13, K2).
Step 2, pressure. The blocked lumen keeps making mucus, and pressure inside the closed tube rises (K24).
Step 3, the wall. Venous congestion and bacterial overgrowth follow, then the mucosa ulcerates and inflammation passes through the wall (K24).

choices.label: Why does pressure matter for blood flow?

say.text: Rising pressure first causes venous congestion, and only then compromises the arterial supply (K24, K25).
Step 4, the pain. Early distension stimulates visceral afferents entering at T10, so the pain is felt **periumbilically** (K26).
Step 5, the shift. When inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, the pain localises to the **right iliac fossa** (K27, K5).
Step 6, the wall dies. The appendicular artery is an **end artery** (K4, K22). When pressure cuts its supply, gangrene follows, then perforation (K25).

choices.label: Why does an end artery matter so much?

say.text: An end artery has no backup route. Once its flow stops, the wall loses its blood supply and gangrene follows (K4, K22).
Case 2, a 45-year-old man. A CT shows an appendicolith (K15) and the lumen is blocked. The pressure is rising.
You take the next step yourself. Which happens first?

choices.label: Arterial compromise comes first, then venous congestion
Venous congestion comes first, then arterial compromise
Wall ischaemia starts before the lumen is blocked
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go back to the pressure step. Which vessel system does rising pressure reach first, the veins or the arteries?
Tempting: arterial supply is what gangrene needs, so arterial failure feels like the first thing to go.
But gangrene is the end of the chain. What does the pressure reach before the arteries?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the chain again: the end point is easy to remember and easy to place too early.

say.text: Pressure first causes venous congestion; the arterial supply fails only after that (K24, K25). Gangrene is the end point, not the start.
Tempting: the wall is where the disease lives, so its failure feels like the first event.
But the lumen is blocked first. Which step came before the wall's blood supply in the chain you traced?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the order: the wall is where the disease is seen, not where it starts.

say.text: Obstruction starts the chain. Pressure builds, and the wall's blood supply fails only after that (K13, K24, K25).
Yes. Pressure first congests the veins, then compromises the arteries, and gangrene follows (K24, K25).
Case 3, with more left to you. Obstruction comes first and perforation last.
Order the four events in the middle.

choices.label: Arterial compromise, rising pressure, venous congestion, gangrene
Rising pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, gangrene
Rising pressure, arterial compromise, venous congestion, gangrene
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pressure comes before anything it damages. Which structure did you trace first in case 2, the veins or the arteries?
Tempting: gangrene and arterial failure are the dramatic events, so they feel like they belong early.
But they sit at the end of the chain. Trace cause to effect again, one step at a time.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so slow down: the dramatic events are the end of the chain, not its start.

say.text: Pressure congests the veins, then compromises the arteries, and gangrene and perforation come last (K24, K25).
Right. Each step drives the next: pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, then gangrene (K24, K25).
Now the symptoms you hear on the ward round.
In typical appendicitis, which order do the symptoms come in?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start from the lumen you just traced. Which symptom does a blocked, distending appendix produce first?
Tempting: vomiting feels like the opening symptom of any gut illness, so it looks like the first thing to appear.
But in appendicitis, what does the distending lumen stimulate first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the order: vomiting is common, but it does not open this story.

say.text: The distended lumen gives pain first (K26). Anorexia is almost constant, and nausea with a few vomits follows the pain (K31). Fever is low-grade (K32).
Yes. Pain first, then vomiting, then a low-grade fever: Murphy's sequence (K6, K31, K32).
A young adult vomited several times through the morning, then got diffuse abdominal pain and loose stools.
Does this make appendicitis more likely or less likely?

choices.label: More likely: vomiting is the typical first symptom
Less likely: the vomiting came before the pain
More likely: fever and vomiting come before pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which symptom came first in this patient, and where that symptom sits in the sequence you just learned.
Tempting: vomiting feels like the first symptom of any abdominal illness, so the story looks like an early one.
But which symptom does the sequence put first in appendicitis?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the order as your filter: pain first, not vomiting.

say.text: Vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis, because appendicitis starts with pain (K6). Fever is low-grade, not an early sign (K32).
Right. Vomiting before the pain points away from appendicitis (K6). Pain-first is your filter.
